claim: A hypoparathyroidism patient with the R25C homozygous mutation has high bone mineral density.
source: In the pursuit of safer osteoporosis treatments, we investigated R25CPTH, a PTH variant wherein the native arginine at position 25 is substituted by cysteine. These studies were prompted by our finding of high bone mineral density in a hypoparathyroidism patient with the R25C homozygous mutation
evidence: The manuscript states this finding directly in the abstract, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 shows TBS reports demonstrating significantly elevated BMD in the lumbar spine and femur of the patient.

claim: R25CPTH(1–84) forms dimers both intracellularly and extracellularly.
source: Our findings indicate that R25CPTH(1–84) forms dimers both intracellularly and extracellularly
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 1D shows both monomeric and dimeric forms of R25CPTH(1–84)-3xFLAG in cell lysate and conditioned medium under non-reduced conditions.

claim: Dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) exhibits altered activity in PTH1R-mediated cyclic AMP (cAMP) response.
source: the synthetic dimeric peptide, R25CPTH(1–34), exhibits altered activity in PTH1R-mediated cyclic AMP (cAMP) response
evidence: Figure 2B shows dose-response curves demonstrating that dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) has reduced potency for cAMP signaling compared to PTH(1–34) in SGS-72 cells.

claim: A single injection of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) induced acute calcemic and phosphaturic responses comparable to PTH(1–34) in mice.
source: Upon a single injection in mice, dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) induced acute calcemic and phosphaturic responses comparable to PTH(1–34).
evidence: Figure 3 shows that both PTH(1–34) and dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) significantly elevated ionized calcium levels at 1-2 hr post-injection and increased urine phosphate levels.

claim: Repeated daily injections of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) increased calvarial bone thickness in intact mice.
source: Furthermore, repeated daily injections increased calvarial bone thickness in intact mice
evidence: Figure 4 shows histological sections and quantification demonstrating significant increase in new bone width following injections of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) compared to vehicle group.

claim: Repeated daily injections of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) improved trabecular and cortical bone parameters in ovariectomized (OVX) mice.
source: Furthermore, repeated daily injections increased calvarial bone thickness in intact mice and improved trabecular and cortical bone parameters in ovariectomized (OVX) mice, akin to PTH(1–34).
evidence: Figures 5 and 6 show μ-CT analysis and histomorphometric data demonstrating improvements in bone parameters in OVX mice treated with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34).

claim: Osteoporosis has a global prevalence of 23.1% among women and 11.7% among men.
source: Recent meta-analysis of previous studies indicates a global osteoporosis prevalence of 23.1% among women and 11.7% among men (Sözen et al., 2017; Salari et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to meta-analysis studies by Sözen et al., 2017 and Salari et al., 2021.

claim: PTH has an exceptionally short half-life in the blood of approximately 2–4 min.
source: PTH has an exceptionally short half-life in the blood of approximately 2–4 min (Bieglmayer et al., 2002; Maier et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Bieglmayer et al., 2002 and Maier et al., 1998.

claim: Long-term administration of a PTH anabolic agent can lead to bone overgrowth, osteosarcoma, as well as hypercalcemia in rodents.
source: It is also worth noting that studies in rodents reveal that long-term administration of a PTH anabolic agent can lead to bone overgrowth, osteosarcoma, as well as hypercalcemia (Vahle et al., 2002; Appelman-Dijkstra and Papapoulos, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Vahle et al., 2002 and Appelman-Dijkstra and Papapoulos, 2016.

claim: PTH is produced and secreted by the parathyroid glands as a straight-chain monomeric polypeptide of 84 amino acids.
source: PTH is produced and secreted by the parathyroid glands as a straight-chain monomeric polypeptide of 84 amino acids (Moallem et al., 1998; Silver et al., 1985; Chen and Goodman, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Moallem et al., 1998, Silver et al., 1985, and Chen and Goodman, 2004.

claim: PTH1R is a class B G protein-coupled receptor.
source: It plays a vital role in maintaining calcium and phosphate equilibrium by acting on the PTH1R, a class B G protein-coupled receptor (Habener et al., 1984; Veldurthy et al., 2016; Kiela and Ghishan, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Habener et al., 1984, Veldurthy et al., 2016, and Kiela and Ghishan, 2009.

claim: PTH1R is expressed primarily in cells of bone and kidney.
source: that is expressed primarily in cells of bone and kidney (Jüppner et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to study by Jüppner et al., 1991.

claim: PTH activates intracellular G proteins, most prominently Gsα.
source: Central to the PTH signaling cascade is the activation of intracellular G proteins (Gardella and Jüppner, 2000), most prominently Gsα
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to study by Gardella and Jüppner, 2000.

claim: Gsα activation leads to the synthesis of the second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP) and the activation of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA).
source: which in turn activates transmembrane adenylyl cyclases, leading to the synthesis of the second messenger cyclic AMP (cAMP), and the activation of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) (Weinstein et al., 2001; Feinstein et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Weinstein et al., 2001 and Feinstein et al., 2011.

claim: PTH can activate Gαq/phospholipase C/inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, diacylglycerol, and protein kinase C signaling pathways.
source: PTH can also activate other second messenger cascades, including the Gαq/phospholipase C/inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, diacylglycerol, and protein kinase C signaling pathways (Iida-Klein et al., 1997; Dunlay and Hruska, 1990)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Iida-Klein et al., 1997 and Dunlay and Hruska, 1990.

claim: PTHrP shares considerable sequence homology with PTH in the first 34 amino acids.
source: PTHrP shares considerable sequence homology with PTH in the first 34 amino acids, which encompass the receptor-binding portions of the two respective ligands.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTH and PTHrP structure.

claim: The PTH1R can adopt at least two distinct ligand-binding conformations, RG and R0.
source: Pharmacologically, the PTH1R can adopt at least two distinct ligand-binding conformations, RG and R0, the selectivity for which can lead to altered modes of signaling in vitro and in vivo for peptides such as PTH, PTHrP, and various hybrid analogs (Okazaki et al., 2008; Pioszak et al., 2009; Cheloha et al., 2015; Hoare et al., 2001; Dean et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Okazaki et al., 2008, Pioszak et al., 2009, Cheloha et al., 2015, Hoare et al., 2001, and Dean et al., 2008.

claim: A patient with chronic hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia has a mutation that changes the arginine at position 25 in the mature PTH(1–84) polypeptide to cysteine (R25CPTH).
source: The current study extends our prior investigation in which we identified in a patient with chronic hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia with a mutation that changes the arginine at position 25 in the mature PTH(1–84) polypeptide to cysteine (R25CPTH) (Lee et al., 2015; Bae et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies by Lee et al., 2015 and Bae et al., 2016.

claim: R25CPTH mutant protein is present in the patient's blood at markedly elevated levels.
source: Antibody assays revealed the R25CPTH mutant protein to be present in the patient's blood at markedly elevated levels.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from antibody assays, referencing prior work.

claim: The introduction of a sole new cysteine within the polypeptide chain of R25CPTH(1–84) might induce homologous bimolecular dimerization through a disulfide bond.
source: We considered the possibility that the introduction of a sole new cysteine within the polypeptide chain of R25CPTH(1–84) might induce homologous bimolecular dimerization through a disulfide bond involving the thiol functional group in each monomer (Banerjee and Lazar, 2001; Trivedi et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies by Banerjee and Lazar, 2001 and Trivedi et al., 2009, and represents a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: Western blot analysis demonstrated the presence of both a low molecular weight monomeric and a higher molecular weight dimeric form of R25CPTH(1–84)-3xFLAG in cell lysate and extracellular conditioned medium.
source: The results demonstrated the presence of both a low molecular weight monomeric, and in the non-reduced samples, a higher molecular weight dimeric form of the R25CPTH(1–84)-3XFLAG protein in both the cell lysate and extracellular conditioned medium fractions
evidence: Figure 1D shows western blot results demonstrating both monomeric and dimeric forms under different conditions.

claim: The dimer of R25CPTH(1–84) appeared to be at an elevated proportion in the medium relative to the lysate.
source: and the dimer appeared to be at an elevated proportion in the medium relative to the lysate (Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows western blot results where the dimeric form is more prominent in the medium samples.

claim: The expression level of R25CPTH(1–84) was higher than that of wild-type PTH(1–84) in both cell lysate and medium.
source: We observed in the above studies that the expression level of R25CPTH(1–84) was higher than that of wild-type PTH(1–84) in both cell lysate and medium
evidence: This observation is stated based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The difference in expression levels between wild-type PTH(1–84) and R25CPTH(1–84) is not related to a difference in sensitivity to proteasome-mediated degradation.
source: The results indicated that while the expression level of wild-type PTH was increased by MG132 treatment, it did not reach the level of R25CPTH, suggesting that the difference in expression is not related to a difference in sensitivity to proteasome-mediated degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3 shows results from proteasome inhibition assay with MG132.

claim: R25CPTH(1–84) secreted outside the cells predominantly exists in dimeric form.
source: Overall, we have confirmed that R25CPTH(1–84) can form a dimeric structure, and the R25CPTH(1–84) secreted outside the cells predominantly exists in dimeric form.
evidence: This conclusion is based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 1D showing higher proportion of dimer in medium.

claim: Monomeric R25CPTH(1–34) bound to both the R0 and RG conformations with comparable, albeit slightly weaker affinity as compared to PTH(1–34).
source: The results revealed that monomeric R25CPTH(1–34) bound to both the R0 and RG conformations with comparable, albeit slightly weaker affinity as compared to PTH(1–34)
evidence: Figure 2A shows competition binding assay results for R0 and RG conformations.

claim: Dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) bound to each conformation with weaker affinity than did the monomeric form while showing an apparent selectivity for higher binding to the RG versus R0 conformation of PTH1R.
source: while dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) bound to each conformation with weaker affinity than did the monomeric form while showing an apparent selectivity for higher binding to the RG versus R0 conformation of PTH1R (Figure 2A).
evidence: Figure 2A shows competition binding assay results demonstrating differential binding to R0 and RG conformations.

claim: Each ligand (PTH(1–34), monomeric R25CPTH(1–34), and dimeric R25CPTH(1–34)) dose-dependently increased the cAMP levels in SGS-72 cells.
source: These assays revealed that each ligand dose-dependently increased the cAMP levels in the cells, detected as an increase in luminescence in an Envision plate reader
evidence: Figure 2B shows dose-response curves for cAMP signaling.

claim: The potencies for cAMP signaling were moderately and more substantially reduced for the monomeric and dimeric forms of R25CPTH(1–34), respectively, as compared to PTH(1–34), but the maximum response attained by each ligand was comparable.
source: and while the potencies were moderately and more substantially reduced for the monomeric and dimeric forms of the ligand, respectively, as compared to PTH(1–34), the maximum response attained by each ligand was comparable (Figure 2B).
evidence: Figure 2B shows dose-response curves demonstrating reduced potency but similar maximal response.

claim: Both PTH(1–34) and dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) induced increases in blood Ca2+ levels that were significant at 1 and 2 hr post-injection, and the levels then returned to the baseline levels by 4 hr.
source: Both PTH(1–34) and dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) induced increases in blood Ca2+ levels that were significant, relative to the levels in vehicle-injected mice, at 1 and 2 hr post-injection, and the levels then returned to the baseline levels of vehicle control mice by 4 hr (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows plasma ionized calcium levels over time after injection.

claim: PTH(1–34) induced a significant decrease in plasma Pi at 1 hr post-injection, and the levels subsequently returned to baseline by 2 hr.
source: PTH(1–34) induced a significant decrease in plasma Pi at 1 hr post-injection, and the levels subsequently returned to baseline by 2 hr.
evidence: Figure 3B shows plasma phosphate levels over time after injection.

claim: Injection of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) resulted in a slight decrease in plasma Pi at 2 hr post-injection, but the effect was not significant.
source: Injection of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) resulted in a slight decrease in plasma Pi at 2 hr post-injection, but the effect was not significant (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3B shows plasma phosphate levels over time after injection.

claim: Pi levels in the urine of mice injected with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) were increased significantly at 2 hr post-injection and then gradually returned to baseline levels.
source: Consistent with this trend, Pi levels in the urine of mice injected with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) were increased significantly at 2 hr post-injection and then gradually returned to baseline levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: Figure 3C shows urine phosphate levels over time after injection.

claim: Both PTH(1–34) and dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) significantly increased the width of the new bone area by approximately fourfold, as compared to the vehicle group in calvarial injection model.
source: These analyses revealed that both PTH(1–34) and dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) significantly increased the width of the new bone area by approximately fourfold, as compared to the vehicle group (Figure 4B).
evidence: Figure 4B shows quantification of new bone width in calvarial injection model.

claim: Treatment with PTH(1–34) increased femoral trabecular bone volume fraction (Tb.BV/TV) by 121% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: Quantitative micro-computed tomography (μ-CT) analysis of the femurs obtained from each group revealed that, as compared to OVX+vehicle controls, treatment with PTH(1–34) increased femoral trabecular bone volume fraction (Tb.BV/TV) by 121%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of trabecular bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with PTH(1–34) increased cortical bone volume fraction (Ct.BV/TV) by 128% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: cortical bone volume fraction (Ct.BV/TV) by 128%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with PTH(1–34) increased cortical thickness (Ct.Th) by 115% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: cortical thickness (Ct.Th) by 115%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with PTH(1–34) increased cortical area (Ct.Ar) by 110% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: cortical area (Ct.Ar) by 110%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with PTH(1–34) increased cortical area fraction (Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar) by 118% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: and cortical area fraction (Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar) by 118%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with PTH(1–34) decreased total tissue area (Tt.Ar) by 93% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: while decreased total tissue area (Tt.Ar) by 93% (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) increased Ct.BMD by 104% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: Treatment with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) had similar effects on the femoral cortical bone parameters, as it increased Ct.BMD by 104%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) increased Ct.BV/TV by 125% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: Ct.BV/TV by 125%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) increased Ct.Th by 107% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: Ct.Th by 107%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) increased Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar by 116% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: and Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar by 116%
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: Treatment with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) decreased Tt.Ar by 86% compared to OVX+vehicle controls.
source: while decreased Tt.Ar 86% (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of cortical bone parameters.

claim: The increase in cortical bone BMD was significant with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) but not with PTH(1–34).
source: The increase in cortical bone BMD was significant with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) but not with PTH(1–34)
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements with statistical significance markers.

claim: An increase in femoral trabecular bone was only observed with PTH(1–34) treatment.
source: whereas an increase in femoral trabecular bone was only observed with PTH(1–34).
evidence: Figure 5B shows μ-CT measurements of trabecular bone parameters.

claim: The maximum load parameter was significantly decreased in the femurs from OVX-control versus Sham mice.
source: The maximum load parameter was significantly decreased in the femurs from OVX-control versus Sham mice
evidence: Figure 5C shows three-point bending test results.

claim: The maximum load parameter was significantly increased by treatment with PTH(1–34), but not dimeric R25CPTH(1–34), relative to the OVX-controls.
source: and was significantly increased, relative to the OVX-controls, by treatment with the PTH(1–34), but not dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Figure 5C shows three-point bending test results.

claim: The slope parameter was significantly decreased in the femurs from OVX-control versus Sham mice.
source: The slope parameter was significantly decreased in the femurs from OVX-control versus Sham mice
evidence: Figure 5C shows three-point bending test results.

claim: The slope parameter tended to increase versus OVX-controls by treatment with either PTH(1–34) or R25CPTH(1–34), but the changes were not significant.
source: and tended to increase versus OVX-controls by treatment with either PTH(1–34) or R25CPTH(1–34), but the changes were not significant.
evidence: Figure 5C shows three-point bending test results.

claim: Serum phosphate levels were modestly increased in the OVX mice treated with PTH(1–34) or dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) as compared to with vehicle, but the effect was significant only with PTH(1–34).
source: while serum phosphate levels were modestly increased in the OVX mice treated with PTH(1–34) or dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) as compared to with vehicle, but the effect was significant only with PTH(1–34).
evidence: Figure 5D shows serum phosphate measurements.

claim: The serum levels of CTX-1 were elevated in each of the OVX groups versus the Sham group.
source: The serum levels of CTX-1, a bone resorption marker (Rosen et al., 2000), were elevated in each of the OVX groups versus the Sham group
evidence: Figure 5D shows serum CTX-1 measurements.

claim: Serum CTX-1 levels tended to be lower in the OVX-PTH(1–34) treatment group, but the change relative to OVX-vehicle was not significant.
source: and tended to be lower in the OVX-PTH(1–34) treatment group, but the change relative to OVX-vehicle was not significant (Figure 5D).
evidence: Figure 5D shows serum CTX-1 measurements.

claim: Serum P1NP and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels were significantly increased in dimeric R25CPTH(1–34)-treated group, compared to the OVX-vehicle group.
source: Interestingly, serum P1NP and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) levels were significantly increased in dimeric R25CPTH(1–34)-treated group, compared to the OVX-vehicle group (Pagani et al., 2005; Wheater et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 5D shows serum P1NP and ALP measurements.

claim: TRAP staining revealed an apparent increase in osteoclast activity in bones of the OVX mice, as compared to those in Sham-control mice.
source: Histological staining of proximal tibial sections for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) activity, a marker of osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, revealed an apparent increase in this activity in bones of the OVX mice, as compared to those in Sham-control mice
evidence: Figure 5E shows TRAP staining images.

claim: TRAP staining appeared to be reduced in the tibiae of the OVX mice treated with PTH(1–34).
source: and the TRAP staining appeared to be reduced in the tibiae of the OVX mice treated with PTH(1–34) (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Figure 5E shows TRAP staining images.

claim: There was a significant increase in the osteoclast surface area relative to bone surface area (Oc.S/BS) in the proximal tibiae of the OVX-vehicle mice, relative to that in the Sham-control mice.
source: Further histomorphometric analysis confirmed a significant increase in the osteoclast surface area relative to bone surface area (Oc.S/BS) in the proximal tibiae of the OVX-vehicle mice, relative to that in the Sham-control mice
evidence: Figure 5F shows quantification of osteoclast parameters.

claim: Oc.S/BS was significantly decreased by treatment with PTH(1–34), but not with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34).
source: and this parameter was significantly decreased by treatment with PTH(1–34), but not with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) (Figure 5F).
evidence: Figure 5F shows quantification of osteoclast parameters.

claim: The trabecular bone volume fraction (Tb.BV/TV, %) and trabecular number (Tb.N) were significantly reduced in the OVX-vehicle group, as compared to the Sham group.
source: The trabecular bone volume fraction (Tb.BV/TV, %) and trabecular number (Tb.N) were significantly reduced in the OVX-vehicle group, as compared to the Sham group
evidence: Figure 6B shows quantification of trabecular bone parameters from vertebrae.

claim: Treatment with either PTH(1–34) or dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) resulted in a significant increase in Tb.BV/TV and Tb.N, as well as a concomitant reduction in trabecular separation (Tb.Sp), as compared to the respective parameters in the OVX-vehicle group.
source: and treatment with either PTH(1–34) or dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) resulted in a significant increase in each of these parameters, as well as a concomitant reduction in trabecular separation (Tb.Sp), as compared to the respective parameters in the OVX-vehicle group (Figure 6B).
evidence: Figure 6B shows quantification of trabecular bone parameters from vertebrae.

claim: The trabecular mineral apposition rate (MAR) and cortical MAR were significantly increased in both the OVX-PTH(1–34) and OVX-dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) groups, as compared to in the OVX-vehicle group.
source: The trabecular mineral apposition rate (MAR) and cortical MAR were significantly increased in both the OVX-PTH(1–34) and OVX-dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) groups, as compared to in the OVX-vehicle group
evidence: Figure 6D shows quantification of bone formation parameters.

claim: There was a tendency for an increase in the bone formation rate (BFR/BS) in both the trabecular and cortical bone with either PTH(1–34) or dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) treatment, but the differences were not statistically significant.
source: and although there was a tendency for an increase in the bone formation rate (BFR/BS) in both the trabecular and cortical bone with either PTH(1–34) or dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) treatment, the differences were not statistically significant, as compared to the OVX-control (Figure 6D).
evidence: Figure 6D shows quantification of bone formation parameters.

claim: Injection of dimeric R25CPTH into osteoporotic OVX mice resulted in significant increases in cortical bone in the femurs and trabecular bone in the vertebrae.
source: In summary, injection of dimeric R25CPTH into osteoporotic OVX mice resulted in significant increases in cortical bone in the femurs and trabecular bone in the vertebrae
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Injection of dimeric R25CPTH into osteoporotic OVX mice resulted in significant increases in osteoblast function and serum markers of bone formation, ALP and P1NP.
source: as well as significant increases in osteoblast function and serum markers of bone formation, ALP and P1NP
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Injection of dimeric R25CPTH into osteoporotic OVX mice did not induce excessive bone resorption or hypercalcemia.
source: without inducing excessive bone resorption or hypercalcemia.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figures 5 and 6 showing serum calcium levels within normal range and bone resorption markers.

claim: Synthetic monomeric peptide R25CPTH(1–34), as compared to PTH(1–34), exhibits a moderately diminished PTH1R-binding affinity and decreased cAMP signaling potency in vitro.
source: In our previous studies, we showed that synthetic monomeric peptide, R25CPTH(1–34), as compared to PTH(1–34), exhibits a moderately diminished PTH1R-binding affinity and decreased cAMP signaling potency in vitro
evidence: This refers to findings from previous studies by Lee et al., 2015.

claim: With long-term infusion in mice, monomeric R25CPTH(1–34) leads to only minimal calcemic and phosphaturic effects.
source: and that with long-term infusion in mice, R25CPTH(1–34) leads to only minimal calcemic and phosphaturic effects, which corroborates the hypocalcemia seen in the original patient, despite the significantly elevated levels of R25CPTH in the plasma (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to findings from previous studies by Lee et al., 2015.

claim: Dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) retains signaling functionality at the PTH1R that is characterized by a potency approximately commensurate with its affinity for binding to the RG PTH1R conformation.
source: Dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) thus retains signaling functionality at the PTH1R that is characterized by a potency approximately commensurate with its affinity for binding to the RG PTH1R conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding and signaling data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Dimeric R25CPTH can elicit calcemic and phosphaturic responses in vivo that are consistent with those expected for an injected PTH1R agonist ligand.
source: These results thus indicate that dimeric R25CPTH can elicit calcemic and phosphaturic responses in vivo that are fully with those expected for an injected PTH1R agonist ligand.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) can induce new bone formation in vivo, similar to PTH, despite molecular and structural changes.
source: These findings thus support a capacity of dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) to induce new bone formation in vivo, similar to PTH, despite molecular and structural changes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The increase of Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar with dimeric R25CPTH(1–34) treatment indicates a decrease in bone marrow space.
source: Considering the reduction of Tt.Ar and no change of Ct.Ar compared to the OVX+vehicle controls, the increase of Ct.Ar/Tt.Ar indicates a decrease in bone marrow space.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the μ-CT data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Arg25 resides in the 20–34 (C-terminal region) of PTH(1–34), which plays a significant role in the binding of the ligand to the extracellular domain (ECD) of the PTH1R.
source: Arg25 resides in the 20–34 (C-terminal region) of PTH(1–34), which plays a significant role in the binding of the ligand to the extracellular domain (ECD) of the PTH1R.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PTH structure-function relationships.

claim: The N-terminal portion of PTH engages the transmembrane domain of the PTH1R, inducing the conformational changes involved in G protein coupling and cAMP production.
source: In concert with the binding of the 20–24 region of PTH to the ECD, the N-terminal portion of PTH engages the transmembrane domain of the PTH1R, inducing the conformational changes involved in G protein coupling and cAMP production (Dean et al., 2008; Clark et al., 2020; Kumar et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2019; Zhai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies by Dean et al., 2008, Clark et al., 2020, Kumar et al., 2016, Zhao et al., 2019, and Zhai et al., 2022.

claim: The precise binding mode used by dimeric R25CPTH to the PTH1R is unknown.
source: The precise binding mode used by dimeric R25CPTH to the PTH1R is unknown
evidence: This is an explicit statement of uncertainty.

claim: The binding mode of dimeric R25CPTH may differ to some extent from that used by the monomeric peptide, due to changes in bulk molecular size and display of accessible functional groups.
source: but it may be anticipated that it differs to some extent from that used by the monomeric peptide, due, for example, to the changes in bulk molecular size and display of accessible functional groups.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on structural considerations.

claim: The receptor conformational changes and the modes of coupling to downstream effectors may differ for the monomeric versus dimeric ligands.
source: Consequently, the receptor conformational changes and the modes of coupling to downstream effectors may differ for the monomeric versus dimeric ligands
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed differences in binding and signaling.

claim: Altered signaling and biological responses in vivo could potentially account for the increased bone density observed in the patient with the homozygous R25CPTH mutation.
source: which could potentially lead to altered signaling and biological responses in vivo. Whether such changes account for the increased bone density observed in the patient with the homozygous R25CPTH mutation remains unknown, but cannot be presently ruled out.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential mechanism.

claim: In OVX mice, PTH and dimeric R25CPTH significantly increased bone formation markers P1NP and ALP.
source: In OVX mice, PTH and dimeric R25CPTH significantly increased bone formation markers P1NP and ALP.
